import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Erdős Problem 970

*References:*
- [erdosproblems.com/970](https://www.erdosproblems.com/970)
- [FGKMT18] Ford, Kevin and Green, Ben and Konyagin, Sergei and Maynard, James and Tao, Terence,
  *Long gaps between primes*. J. Amer. Math. Soc. (2018), 65-105.
- [Iw78] Iwaniec, Henryk, *On the problem of {J}acobsthal*. Demonstratio Math. (1978), 225--231.
-/

namespace Erdos970

/--
`IsJacobsthalBound k m` says that every interval of `m` consecutive integers contains an
integer coprime to every positive natural number having at most `k` distinct prime factors.
-/
def IsJacobsthalBound (k m : ℕ) : Prop :=
  ∀ n : ℕ, 0 < n → n.primeFactors.card ≤ k →
    ∀ a : ℤ, ∃ i : ℕ, i < m ∧ (a + i).natAbs.Coprime n

/--
Jacobsthal's function, uniformly parametrized by the maximum number of distinct prime factors.
-/
noncomputable def jacobsthalFunction (k : ℕ) : ℕ :=
  sInf {m : ℕ | IsJacobsthalBound k m}

/--
Let $h(k)$ be Jacobsthal's function, defined to as the minimal $m$ such that, if $n$ has at most $k$ prime factors, then in any set of $m$ consecutive integers there exists an integer coprime to $n$. Determine the order of magnitude of $h(k)$. In particular, is it true that $$h(k) \ll k^2?$$
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_970 : answer(sorry) ↔
    ∃ C > (0 : ℝ), ∀ k : ℕ, 0 < k → (jacobsthalFunction k : ℝ) ≤ C * k ^ 2 := by
  sorry

end Erdos970

findings.description: The docstring says every interval contains “an integer coprime to every positive natural number” with at most k distinct prime factors. Literally, this requires one common witness for all such n. The Lean definition correctly quantifies n before the existential witness, allowing the coprime integer to depend on n. These readings differ: IsJacobsthalBound 1 2 holds, but the interval {2,3} has no single element coprime to both 2 and 3. Both facts were verified in the scratch file. The Lean mathematics is correct; only the prose reverses the quantifier dependence.
findings.source_evidence: The cited problem page says that “if n has at most k prime factors, then in any set of m consecutive integers there exists an integer coprime to n,” with n fixed before choosing the integer. Read in the archived copy at https://web.archive.org/web/20250901000000id_/https://www.erdosproblems.com/970. Iwaniec, On the problem of Jacobsthal, pp. 225–226, likewise considers elements coprime to a fixed product Q of the chosen primes.
findings.suggested_fix: Rewrite the docstring: “For every positive natural number n having at most k distinct prime factors, every interval of m consecutive integers contains an integer coprime to n.” Leave the Lean definition unchanged.

reformulations.difference: The source asks whether h(k) ≪ k² asymptotically. Lean asks for a positive real constant bounding h(k) by Ck² for every positive natural k.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: A global bound implies the eventual bound. Conversely, an eventual bound extends to all positive k by enlarging its constant to cover the finitely many exceptions; k² is strictly positive at each exceptional positive k. Since h is nonnegative, the norms in the standard big-O definition introduce no change. The equivalence was proved in Lean for every function ℕ → ℕ and specialized to jacobsthalFunction.

review.notes: All three declarations were checked. The theorem faithfully states the source's explicitly singled-out quadratic-upper-bound subquestion. Iwaniec's uniform upper bound ensures the set defining jacobsthalFunction is nonempty, so Nat.sInf's empty-set default is not a defect. Scratch checks in /workspace/review/scratch.lean compile without errors and establish h(0)=1, h(1)=2, failure of every zero-length bound, and equivalence of the index/natAbs formulation with an integer-interval gcd formulation. Small fixed-modulus computations also agree with the expected values. Direct live-source requests were blocked; the problem and Iwaniec paper were read through archival copies. The current independent Erdős database still records problem 970 as open.
